sections.title: Why this module matters
sections.body: Redis is the default choice for caching, session storage, rate limiting, distributed locking, and lightweight pub/sub in Go microservices. The go-redis/redis v9 client is the de-facto standard, offering a context-aware, pipeline-capable, cluster-aware API. Interviewers probe this module to test whether you understand not just the basic GET/SET pattern but the subtleties that matter in production: pipeline batching to reduce RTTs, Lua scripting for atomic multi-key operations, Redlock for distributed locking, and Redis Streams as a durable message queue alternative. Getting these right separates a developer who uses Redis as a cache from one who uses it as a systems primitive.

sections.title: Mental model
sections.body: rdb := redis.NewClient(options) creates a thread-safe client backed by a connection pool; it is safe to share globally. Every command returns a *redis.Cmd (or typed variant like *redis.StringCmd) that carries both the result and an error; always check redis.Nil separately from other errors to distinguish a missing key from a connection failure. Pipelines batch multiple commands into a single round-trip — the client buffers commands and flushes them together, but each command result is checked individually after the flush. Transactions (MULTI/EXEC) can be combined with WATCH for optimistic locking. Lua scripts (EVALSHA) run atomically server-side, making them ideal for check-and-set patterns like rate limiting. Redis Streams offer consumer groups with at-least-once delivery semantics, making them a lightweight alternative to Kafka for intra-service messaging.

sections.title: Must-know concepts
sections.body: 1. redis.NewClient options — Addr, Password, DB, PoolSize, MinIdleConns, DialTimeout, ReadTimeout. 2. redis.Nil — sentinel error for a missing key; treat it as a cache miss, not a failure. 3. Pipeline vs TxPipeline — Pipeline sends commands in batch without atomicity; TxPipeline wraps in MULTI/EXEC for atomicity. 4. WATCH / Optimistic locking — watch keys before a TxPipeline; if any watched key changes the transaction is aborted and you retry. 5. Lua scripting with redis.NewScript — script is cached server-side by SHA, executed atomically; KEYS and ARGV are the idiomatic parameter conventions. 6. Pub/Sub — Subscribe returns a *redis.PubSub; read messages in a goroutine via ps.Channel(); fan-out to multiple subscribers works but delivery is fire-and-forget (no persistence). 7. Redis Streams — XADD produces, XREADGROUP + consumer group provides at-least-once with acknowledgement via XACK. 8. Distributed lock (Redlock) — SET key value NX PX ttl atomically; release with a Lua script that checks ownership before DEL.

sections.title: Likely interview hooks
sections.body: Q: What is the difference between Pipeline and TxPipeline in go-redis? — Both batch commands; TxPipeline wraps them in MULTI/EXEC so all commands execute atomically or none do. Q: Why use a Lua script for rate limiting instead of a GET-then-SET sequence? — GET and SET are two separate round-trips; between them another request can interleave. Lua runs atomically on the Redis server, making the check-and-increment race-free. Q: How do you implement a distributed lock in Go with Redis? — SET key token NX PX 5000 acquires the lock; release with a Lua script that checks the token before deleting, preventing a different process from releasing a lock it doesn't own. Q: When would you use Redis Streams over Pub/Sub? — Streams persist messages and support consumer groups with acknowledgement; Pub/Sub is ephemeral — subscribers that disconnect miss all messages published while offline. Q: How does redis.Nil differ from a network error? — redis.Nil means the key does not exist (expected, handle as a cache miss); a network error means the client could not reach Redis (unexpected, handle as a failure).

sections.title: Speaking template
sections.body: "I treat the go-redis client as a long-lived singleton with pool settings calibrated to our concurrency — typically PoolSize set to the number of goroutines that can concurrently hit Redis. For any operation that reads and conditionally writes I reach for a Lua script rather than a pipeline, because Lua gives me atomicity without MULTI/EXEC overhead; that's how I implement our token-bucket rate limiter. For distributed locking I use the SET NX PX pattern with a random token as the value, and I release with a Lua script that checks ownership before deleting — that prevents a slow lock holder from accidentally releasing a lock that's already been re-acquired. When I need durable, ordered message delivery between services I use Redis Streams with consumer groups rather than Pub/Sub, because Streams survive a subscriber restart and support XACK so I know exactly what's been processed."
